catalog_quote: STRESS. The stress system of Ojibwe has been analyzed by a number of researchers (Bloomfield 1958, Rhodes 1976, Valentine 1985, etc.). Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical. Very similar stress systems have been proposed for other Algonquian languages, e.g., Passamaquoddy (Stowell 1979). In southeastern dialects of Ojibwe, a very prominent rule of weak vowel syncope is resulting in a restructuring of much of the lexicon and the form of inflectional person prefixes on verbs and nouns. In other dialects, such as Berens River Ojibwe, the same quantity-sensitive iambic metrical patterns are evident, but the correlate of stress in these dialects is pitch, resulting in alter…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Eastern Ojibwa (east2542) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had a single title item, Glottolog ref 688395 'Stress in Border Lakes Ojibwe' (2003), which Glottolog lists author-less under the volume editor H.C. Wolfart and tags with language code east2542. The Carleton OJS landing page (article 413) identifies the author as Bonnie Swierzbin (Papers of the 34th Algonquian Conference, pp. 341-370); the open PDF was downloaded from https://ojs.library.carleton.ca/index.php/ALGQP/article/download/413/317 The paper is an instrumental study of Border Lakes Ojibwe, a NON-syncopating dialect on the Ontario-Minnesota border (Seine River consultants), which the author calls a 'southern dialect' and Glottolog geography places under Northwestern Ojibwa (nort2961/rain1239) - it is not Eastern Ojibwa, so the Glottolog language tag is a misassignment. Its findings (p. 367): iambs left-to-right, no degenerate feet, binary right-headed cola, primary stress on the rightmost non-final heavy syllable except HH' words. Its only statements about Eastern Ojibwa/Odawa are second-hand (Kaye 1973, Piggott 1980/1983, Hayes 1995; pp. 357-358: Odawa primary stress on the penultimate stressed vowel with two stressed vowels, antepenultimate with three or more). No first-hand Eastern Ojibwa stress statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title (no new stress statement was found); our earlier reading's Valentine 1996 / Rhodes 1976 / Chamberlain 1892 / SPA-1979-on-Bloomfield material in the same folder remains the best. Nothing to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title (priority none). lookups were done by automated download against Glottolog and Carleton OJS.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive iambic feet are built left to right from the start of the word: a short-vowel syllable is weak and the next syllable is strong; a long-vowel syllable is always strong (it can never be the weak member); the final syllable is treated as extrametrical. Strong syllables are stressed, weak ones unstressed; in Eastern Ojibwa/Odawa (the 'southeastern dialects') the weak short vowels are syncopated. Valentine 1996 does not say which strong syllable carries primary word stress; for Odawa, Piggott 1980/1983 and Kaye 1973 (via Chambers 1979 and Swierzbin 2003) put it on the antepenultimate stressed syllable in words with three or more stressed vowels, otherwise on the first (penultimate) stressed one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not separated from primary stress in Valentine 1996: every foot head (each long vowel and each even-numbered short vowel counting from the left) is prominent; the Odawa literature (Piggott 1983 pp. 81-83) treats all such syllables plus the word-final syllable as stressed, with one of them promoted to main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Final syllable extrametrical; northern dialects (e.g. Severn) show stress shifts in sequences of short vowels; Berens River uses pitch rather than intensity as the correlate; Piggott notes CVNCV disyllables with initial stress in Odawa; Chamberlain 1892 (Mississauga of Scugog) reported no fixed accent rule and 'practically no accent' in most disyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolation forms; the statement is made for Ojibwe as a whole (all dialects) and explicitly extends to the syncopating southeastern dialects that include Eastern Ojibwa; the SPA 1979 database entry for Eastern Ojibwa (reading Bloomfield 1957) states that Bloomfield does not mention word stress but describes reduction of short vowels in odd-numbered non-final syllables, which is the same iambic pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted Valentine 1996 statement is made for Ojibwe as a whole (all dialects, Glottolog nuclear-Ojibwe group cent2252 and beyond) and applies to Eastern Ojibwa as one of the 'southeastern dialects' with weak-vowel syncope; it is not a description of east2542 alone. The primary-stress placement (antepenultimate stressed syllable) comes only from the Odawa literature (Kaye 1973, Piggott 1980/1983; otta1242, already in the catalog), and Valentine 2001 treats Odawa and Eastern Ojibwe together as Nishnaabemwin. Chamberlain 1892 describes the Mississauga (Scugog) variety of Eastern Ojibwa; Rhodes 1976 (diss.) calls the Walpole Island / Wikwemikong dialect 'Central Ojibwa' but identifies it with Bloomfield's Eastern Ojibwa.

Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel. sources.note: Section STRESS pp. 312-314: pan-Ojibwe system of quantity-sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge (weak-strong; weak position only a short vowel), final syllable often extrametrical; southeastern dialects (Eastern Ojibwe/Odawa) syncopate metrically weak short vowels; some northern dialects use pitch as the stress correlate or show stress shifts in short-vowel sequences. No statement of where primary stress falls.

III 'Accent and Syllabification', pp. 13-14: accent and syllabification 'subject to not a little variation, seemingly at the caprice of the speaker'; root accent in dissyllables 'by no means always the case'; 'Nor does there appear to be any absolute rule for the accentuation of polysyllables'; in most dissyllables 'the stress is so evenly distributed that there is practically no accent'. sources.citation: Piggott, Glyne L. 1983. Extrametricality and Ojibwa stress. McGill Working Papers in Linguistics 1(1): 80-117.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Data 'primarily from the Odawa (i.e. Ottawa) dialect' (p. 80). SPE-style review pp. 81-83: every long vowel stressed; alternating stress on even-numbered short vowels left to right; the final syllable of every word is stressed; minor rule stressing the first vowel of CVNCV disyllables; main stress on the antepenultimate stressed vowel (Piggott 1980 via Swierzbin 2003 in the otta1242 record). Odawa, not Eastern Ojibwa proper.
